title: Playing Countdown, Satellite and Giant Steps; Coltrane devices
summary: He thinks changes on Countdown, uses worked-out devices, discusses transcribing Coltrane and practices by hearing tunes in his head.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: It makes, technology seems to me, in my generation, it seems to make things a little too easy or something. Well, time does go by. I was listening to you play today and I’m trying to get a handle on what you think about, if you’re playing a tune like let’s say “Countdown,” it’s pretty darn hard and the tempo is pretty bright. Are the chord changes going by in your head? And are you trying to choose notes from them?

Well in “Countdown” [inaudible] I had to play it once with a band. I’ve gone through “Countdown,” I’ve gone through “Satellite.” I like to play “Satellite.” I like to play “Giant Steps,” so I’m familiar with that, but “Countdown” is actually the hardest song I think. It’s more difficult. Because people like to play it like [scats]. I’m singing “Satellite,” but anyway “Countdown” the tempo is like [scats] and the changes move really quick. So yeah, I do think about the changes and I do actually have things worked out basically, I have devices worked out and so those moments when I may try to be creative and then the creativity leaves me because it’s so hard. I can go back to the devices. And to play a tune like “Countdown” you really have to have a lot of devices. Because you know I transcribed Coltrane’s second solo [inaudible] a month later, in fact it was called “Countdown” and he played all the same tunes again, and I transcribed that one. And Trane does the same thing. He has devices that he plays over and over again but he has so many of them and he’s so diverse, you know he has not an unlimited supply but he has a lot of devices because it doesn’t sound like he’s doing it. But if you transcribe that solo you can see the things he’s worked out, the way he gets through things. The same thing with “Satellite.” And “Giant Steps” is my favorite. I think that he plays so creatively on “Giant Steps.” There are some things that he repeats here and there but there are also times on “Giant Steps,” especially the second one, where he just seems like he found it right there on the tape. It’s a little disjointed in the rhythms, like the rhythm is © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-
a little stronger because he’s slipping and sliding around and it’s like wow, that’s really beautiful.
I guess that’s what transcription does for you. It really spotlights those moments where he’s not quite where he wants to be and then bam, he launches into it.

Yeah, to answer your question on a tune like “Countdown” I definitely play with the changes. That’s actually that’s a good way that’s the only way to practice for me. If you get a tempo in my head, you just listen to the changes go by in my head without a recording. So I’ll maybe get the tune in my head, playing it on the piano or listening to the record and then just sit in a chair and see the tune going by in my head. It’s good training. Because when you’re playing that’s what you have to do. So it’s good to see the tune just keep going by in your head, intently.
